Lesson Overview

In our last lesson, we explored Product End-of-Life Analysis — thinking about what happens to products after they've served their purpose. Today, we're taking that thinking a step further by focusing on Sustainable Materials within the Creationeering™ phase of Death & Recycling.

This topic connects directly to your mousetrap car project. Every component — from the chassis to the wheels — has an origin and an end. By learning about sustainable materials, you'll be equipped to make thoughtful decisions that not only make your car perform well but also respect the world God has entrusted to us. You'll consider how your car's parts can be recycled, reused, or even biodegraded, making your design a testament to responsible engineering.

Learning Objectives

Students will be able to:

  • Define sustainable materials and explain their importance in engineering design.
  • Identify at least three different end-of-life options for materials used in their mousetrap cars.
  • Apply criteria for recyclability and reusability when selecting components for their mousetrap car.
  • Explain how macro-level material choices connect to atomic-level properties and environmental impact through multiscale modeling.
  • Articulate how responsible material selection aligns with biblical principles of stewardship — tending and keeping the creation God has entrusted to us.

items.definition: Materials that can be produced, used, and disposed of without harming the environment or depleting natural resources for future generations.
The process of converting waste materials into new materials and objects.
Using an item again for its original purpose or a different purpose without significant alteration.
Transforming discarded items or waste materials into products of higher quality or value than the original.
Recycling a material in such a way that the new product is of lower quality or functionality than the original.
A traditional economic model where products are made from raw materials, used, and then disposed of as waste.
An economic model designed to minimize waste and make the most of resources by keeping products and materials in use for as long as possible.

data.html:
Tending and Keeping God's Creation

Our journey as engineers begins with a foundational command. In Genesis 2:15, God placed humanity in the garden "to work it and take care of it." That phrase — tend and keep — isn't just about gardening. It's a blueprint for how we interact with everything God has made.

Think of God as the ultimate Designer. He built an incredibly complex, self-sustaining system and then handed us the keys, saying: manage this well. That's stewardship. And stewardship shows up in engineering every time you decide what material to use, how long it will last, and where it goes when you're done with it.

When you choose materials for your mousetrap car, you're not just solving a physics problem. You're participating in that original calling — to cultivate, manage, and preserve the resources we've been given. Good engineering and good stewardship are not in conflict. They're the same thing.

Genesis 2:15 (NIV): "The Lord God took the man and put him in the Garden of Eden to work it and take care of it."

This verse is a design brief from God Himself. To work creation means to develop and build. To take care of it means to protect and preserve. As a Creationeer, both sides of that command live inside every design decision you make.

The Lifecycle of Materials — Beyond the Finish Line

When you're designing your mousetrap car, it's easy to focus on race day. Will it go far? Will it go straight? Those questions matter. But a true Creationeer thinks beyond the finish line.

Every material in your car has a story that starts before you ever touch it and continues long after the race is over. That full story — from raw resource to final disposal — is called a material's lifecycle. Understanding it changes the way you design.

Here's a simple way to think about it: imagine a straight line versus a circle. In a linear economy, resources travel in one direction — extract, make, use, throw away. Most of the value gets buried in a landfill. In a circular economy, materials loop back. They're designed to be reused, recycled, or returned to nature safely. The goal is to keep resources in play as long as possible, just like a well-maintained tool that gets passed down through generations.

data.html:
End-of-Life Options for Your Materials

When a product reaches the end of its useful life, it doesn't have to become trash. Engineers think carefully about end-of-life options during the design phase — not after. Here are the main paths a material can take:

  • Reuse: The simplest option. Can the part be used again as-is? A wooden axle or a plastic bottle cap wheel might find a second life in another project without any processing at all.
  • Upcycling: Taking a used material and turning it into something of greater value. A scrap piece of aluminum from your car's chassis becomes part of a decorative frame — same material, higher purpose.
  • Recycling (Downcycling): Most recycling is actually downcycling. Plastic gets melted down and reformed, but each cycle usually degrades the material's quality slightly. It's still far better than a landfill, but it's not a perfect loop.
  • Composting / Biodegradation: For organic or biodegradable materials, returning them to the earth is a valid and elegant solution. A balsa wood chassis, for example, will eventually break down naturally.
  • Landfill (last resort): When no other option exists. Good engineering minimizes how often a material ends up here.

Applying This to Your Mousetrap Car

Now let's make this concrete. Your mousetrap car is built from several types of materials — wood, plastic, metal, rubber, and maybe some cardboard or foam. Each one has a different recyclability profile.

When you're selecting materials, ask yourself these three questions:

  • Where did this come from? Is it a renewable resource (like wood) or a finite one (like most plastics)?
  • How long will it last? A durable material used once and trashed is still wasteful. Design for longevity or for easy disassembly.
  • Where will it go? Can this part be recycled locally? Is it biodegradable? Or is it headed straight to a landfill the moment the project ends?

These aren't just environmental questions — they're engineering questions. The best designs account for the full lifecycle, not just peak performance.

data.html:
From the Macro to the Micro — Multiscale Thinking

Here's something that might surprise you: the choices you make at the design table — what material to use, how thick to cut a piece of wood — are connected all the way down to the atomic level.

This idea is called multiscale modeling. It means that engineers think about how decisions at one scale (the big picture) affect what happens at another scale (the microscopic or even atomic level). When you pick a material, you're also picking its molecular structure, its bonds, and how those bonds behave under stress or heat.

For example, a plastic wheel might look identical to a wooden one at race-day scale. But at the atomic level, plastic is made of long polymer chains derived from petroleum. It doesn't biodegrade. Wood, on the other hand, is made of cellulose — a natural polymer that living organisms can break down. Same function at the macro level; completely different story at the micro level.

Great engineers connect both scales in their thinking. Your material choice is never just about how something looks or performs today — it's about what those atoms will be doing in a landfill fifty years from now.

Design tip: When choosing materials for your mousetrap car, prioritize components that can be separated easily at the end of the project. Gluing unlike materials together (like metal to plastic) makes recycling nearly impossible. Mechanical fasteners — screws, clips, friction fits — allow for clean disassembly and better end-of-life options.

Sustainable Material Selection in Practice

Let's look at some of the common mousetrap car materials side by side and think about them through a sustainability lens:

  • Balsa wood (chassis/frame): Renewable, lightweight, biodegradable. Excellent sustainable choice. Can be composted after use.
  • CD/DVD wheels: Made from polycarbonate plastic — not easily recycled in most curbside programs. Reuse is the best option here. Can they be used again in another project?
  • Metal axles (steel or aluminum): Both are highly recyclable. Steel and aluminum retain their properties through many recycling cycles — true circular economy materials.
  • Rubber bands: Natural rubber is biodegradable; synthetic rubber is not. Worth considering which type you're using.
  • Cardboard: Highly recyclable and biodegradable. One of the most sustainable structural materials available.

Notice a pattern? Materials that come from nature (wood, natural rubber, cardboard) tend to have cleaner end-of-life stories. Metals are excellent because they recycle without significant quality loss. Plastics are the trickiest — useful in performance, but challenging at end of life.

Common mistake: Assuming that something labeled "recyclable" will actually be recycled. A material is only truly recycled if your local facility accepts it and processes it correctly. When you research your materials, check what recycling infrastructure actually exists in your area — not just what the label says.

Bringing It Together — Design with the End in Mind

Sustainable engineering isn't about sacrificing performance. It's about expanding your definition of what "good design" means. A mousetrap car that travels far is a success. A mousetrap car that travels far and is built from materials that can be recovered, reused, or returned to the earth safely? That's excellent engineering — and excellent stewardship.

Every time you pick up a material and ask, "Where will this go when I'm done with it?" you're thinking like a Creationeer. You're connecting your work to something bigger than a single race. You're honoring the mandate to tend and keep the creation you've been given.

That's not a burden. That's a privilege.

data.title: Going Deeper: What Is a Life Cycle Assessment (LCA)?
data.html:
Professional engineers use a formal tool called a Life Cycle Assessment (LCA) to measure the total environmental impact of a product from raw material extraction all the way through disposal. It accounts for energy use, water consumption, carbon emissions, and waste generated at every stage.

LCAs are used by companies designing everything from running shoes to smartphones to airplane parts. The goal is to find the stage in the lifecycle where the biggest environmental costs occur — and then redesign to reduce them.

You won't run a full LCA on your mousetrap car, but you're practicing the same kind of thinking every time you trace a material back to its source and forward to its end. That intuition is the foundation of the formal LCA process.
